o:
A subarray is Fibonacci-like if every element from the third onward equals the sum of the previous two. Any subarray of length 1 or 2 qualifies automatically. Because the property is defined on contiguous windows and each window's validity is determined by consecutive triples, a single left-to-right scan suffices: extend the current valid window while the Fibonacci condition holds, otherwise restart a fresh window seeded by the last two elements.

Example 1: [1,1,1,1,2,3,5,1] — starting at index 2, the chain 1,1,2,3,5 satisfies the recurrence for 5 elements, then 1 breaks it. Example 3: 1e9+1e9 exceeds nothing in particular but shows why 64-bit care matters in typed languages; the answer stays 2 since the third equal element breaks the strict-sum condition (1e9 != 2e9).
k: Validity of a window depends only on consecutive triples, enabling an O(n) scan
When the condition breaks at index i, the new candidate window starts at i-1 with length 2
Compare via subtraction (nums[i] - nums[i-1] == nums[i-2]) to avoid overflow in 32-bit languages

a.n: Approach 1: Linear Scan with Running Length
a.i: Maintain cur = length of the longest Fibonacci run ending at index i. If nums[i] == nums[i-1] + nums[i-2], extend; otherwise the run resets to length 2 (the pair nums[i-1], nums[i]). Track the maximum.
s: For i from 2 to n-1: if the sum condition holds, cur++; else cur = 2
Update best with cur each iteration; return best
a.t: O(n) — each index is examined once

w: The scan is optimal; a brute force over all O(n^2) windows is unnecessary. Pitfalls: resetting cur to 1 instead of 2 (the previous element still seeds a valid pair), and overflow when summing two 1e9 values in C++/Java — cast to 64-bit or compare differences. Follow-up: report the actual subarray indices by recording the argmax position.
